title: Lees and bâtonnage
what: What happens to the fine yeast sediment after fermentation: leave the wine on it, rack the wine off it, or keep it and stir it back up (bâtonnage).

steps: so sulphury, reduced smells build up; stirring mixes in oxygen and prevents them

choose: Keep stirred fine lees for a barrel-aged Burgundy-style Chardonnay: lees absorb oxygen, soften the woody character and, over months, add subtle bread or biscuit notes. Winemakers credit lees with body; research has not proven it. Rack off for a pure, fruit-led Riesling, or when the wine smells reduced.
exam: Questions ask how lees ageing and stirring change a white wine. Give autolysis → mannoproteins → stability, the subtle bread note, the reduction risk and stirring, and a region.

check.question: A Chardonnay sits unstirred on heavy lees in a large steel tank and starts to smell of struck match. What helps most?
options: Stir the lees or rack the wine off them
Add SO₂: it binds the struck-match smell
Leave it: struck match always fades on lees
Move it into new oak to mask the smell
check.answer: Stir the lees or rack the wine off them
check.why: Settled lees are strongly reductive. Stirring mixes oxygen back in and racking removes the source; SO₂ or masking leaves the cause in place.

simplification: Game simplification: unstirred lees only slow the fading of H₂S already formed; haze and tartrate stability are not modelled; the game adds body for months on lees, which research has not proven.
